question: Three of us own all the shares in our company and we have kept the profits in the business instead of paying dividends. Can the tax service treat those profits as paid out to us, and is there a deadline for doing that?
expected_answer: Where a Nigerian company controlled by not more than five individuals has not distributed its profits, the Service may direct that the part that could have been distributed without harm to the business is treated as distributed (NTA Section 10(1)).
The amount treated as distributed is taxable income of the individual shareholders in proportion to their shareholdings (NTA Section 10(2)).
The direction must be made not later than three years after the Service receives the company's audited accounts for that period (NTA Section 10(6)).
must_not: states that the Service can never treat retained profits as distributed
states a time limit other than three years
rationale: Section 10(1), (2) and (6) answer; three owners is within 'not more than five individuals'.

question: Before our company started trading, we spent two years paying for market research and staff training. Can those start-up costs be deducted once the business begins?
expected_answer: Expenditure incurred within six years before the business commenced, which would have been deductible if incurred after commencement, is treated as incurred on the first day of the business (NTA Section 20(1)(j)).
must_not: states that costs incurred before the business started can never be deducted
states a look-back period other than six years
rationale: Section 20(1)(j) answers, with its condition that the cost would have been deductible after commencement; 20(1) opening words give the wholly and exclusively test.

question: I hire out generators to customers on monthly contracts, and they pay me each month. For VAT, when is each month's supply treated as happening?
expected_answer: Goods supplied under a rental agreement with periodic payments are treated as supplied successively for successive parts of the agreement period (NTA Section 147(3)(a)).
Each successive supply is treated as made when payment becomes due or is received, whichever is earlier (NTA Section 147(3)(a)).
must_not: states that VAT on the whole contract is due when the contract is signed
rationale: Section 147(3)(a) covers rental agreements and overrides 147(1); it is the specific rule for goods rented out on periodic payments. Section 147(3)(b)(i) in the same chunk also covers periodic supplies and adds a third trigger, an invoice relating only to that payment. An answer that applies (b)(i) or adds the invoice trigger is not wrong: it is graded as stating both key points if it gives successive monthly supplies timed by payment falling due or being received.

question: I am bringing machines into Nigeria from China. On what amount is the VAT on the import worked out?
expected_answer: The value of an imported taxable supply is its price plus taxes, duties and other charges levied outside Nigeria or because of importation, other than VAT (NTA Section 150(a)).
Costs such as commission, transport and insurance up to the port or point of entry are also added (NTA Section 150(b)).
must_not: states that VAT is charged on the purchase price alone
rationale: Section 150 answers in full.

question: My company owns and runs a professional football club. Are the club's profits free of company income tax?
expected_answer: The profits of a company engaged in sporting activities are exempt from tax under Chapter Two of the Act (NTA Section 163(1)(r)).
must_not: states that the club's profits are taxed at 30%
rationale: Running a professional football club is a sporting activity; Section 163(1)(r) answers.

question: For the small company test, does my company's gross turnover count only its sales, or also the interest and rent it receives?
expected_answer: Gross turnover covers inflows from operating activities that increase equity, including sales of goods, supply of services, and receipts of interest, rents, royalties or dividends (NTA Section 202, "gross turnover").
It excludes increases that come from contributions by equity participants (NTA Section 202, "gross turnover").
must_not: states that gross turnover means sales only
rationale: The definition lists interest and rents.

question: Does the tax law treat crypto coins and NFTs as digital assets?
expected_answer: Digital assets are digital representations of value that can be digitally exchanged, and include crypto assets, utility tokens, security tokens and non-fungible tokens (NFTs) (NTA Section 202, "digital assets").
must_not: states that NFTs are not digital assets
rationale: The definition names crypto assets and NFTs.

question: We are buying delivery vans on hire purchase and paying in instalments. How much of the cost counts for capital allowances in each period, and who is treated as the owner?
expected_answer: For an asset acquired under hire purchase, qualifying capital expenditure in a basis period is limited to the instalments paid up to that period, excluding any interest (NTA First Schedule, paragraph 2(a)).
The hirer is treated as the owner of the asset (NTA First Schedule, paragraph 2(b)).
must_not: states that the full price of the vans qualifies in the first period
states that the interest in the instalments qualifies
rationale: Paragraph 2 of Part I of the First Schedule answers both parts.

question: We plan to stop trading for about a year and then start again. Do we have to tell the tax authority, and what happens to our Tax ID?
expected_answer: A taxable person that temporarily stops business must notify the relevant tax authority of its intention to suspend its registration within 30 days of stopping (NTAA Section 10(1)).
The authority classifies the Tax ID as dormant and suspends it (NTAA Section 10(2)).
On reapplication the same Tax ID is re-issued (NTAA Section 10(6)).
must_not: states that the Tax ID is cancelled and a new one must be obtained
applies the deregistration rule for a permanent stop
rationale: Section 10(1), (2) and (6) answer a temporary stop.

question: Our company was incorporated eight months ago. When is its first annual income tax return due?
expected_answer: A newly incorporated company must file within 18 months from incorporation or not later than six months after the end of its first accounting period, whichever is earlier (NTAA Section 11(5)(b)).
must_not: gives only the six-months-after-year-end rule for companies in business for more than 18 months
rationale: Section 11(5)(b) applies to a company incorporated eight months ago.

question: I disagree with a tax assessment I have just received. How long do I have to object, and what must my objection include?
expected_answer: An objection is made by written notice to the relevant tax authority asking it to revise the assessment (NTAA Section 41(1)).
It is valid only if delivered within 30 days from the date the notice of assessment was served (NTAA Section 41(2)(a)).

It must give the grounds: the issues disputed with their monetary values, the amendment needed, the justification, the profits or income admitted, and the tax admitted or that none is admitted (NTAA Section 41(2)(b)).
The authority may extend the time for good cause (NTAA Section 41(3)).
must_not: states an objection period other than 30 days
rationale: Section 41(1)-(3) answers both parts.

question: My company, whose yearly turnover is about ₦600 million, should have deducted withholding tax when paying a contractor but forgot to. What administrative penalty can it face?
expected_answer: A person obliged to deduct or withhold tax who fails to do so is liable to an administrative penalty of 40% of the amount not deducted (NTAA Section 105).
must_not: gives the 10% a year penalty for late remittance as the penalty for failing to deduct
rationale: Section 105 answers. Turnover of about ₦600 million is above the ₦100,000,000 small business limit, so the Administration Act Section 22(8) exception for small businesses does not apply.

question: We think we have overpaid company income tax. How long do we have to claim it back, and how soon must a refund be paid?
expected_answer: A refund claim must be made in writing within six years after the end of the year of assessment it relates to (NTAA Section 55(7)).
Overpaid tax is refunded after an audit by the relevant tax authority (NTAA Section 55(1)).
A refund due must be made within 90 days of the authority's decision, with an option of set-off against other tax liability (NTAA Section 55(3)).
must_not: gives the 30-day VAT refund period as the deadline for this refund
states a claim period other than six years
rationale: Section 55(1), (3) and (7) answer.

question: What does section 74 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act cover?
expected_answer: The relevant tax authority may reject an advance ruling application that needs an opinion on foreign law, an issue already before a court or tribunal, the interpretation of the Constitution, an academic, hypothetical, frivolous or vexatious issue, or a ruling that would substantially interfere with an ongoing audit, investigation or proceeding (NTAA Section 74).
must_not: describes section 74 as being about a subject other than rejecting advance ruling applications
rationale: Section 74 is one rule with five grounds.

question: My company sold a set of office chairs as a taxable supply at the standard VAT rate, and the customer paid ₦860,000 including VAT. How much of that payment is VAT?
expected_answer: VAT is charged at 7.5% on the value of taxable supplies (NTA Section 148).
For a money consideration, the value is the amount which, with the VAT added, equals the consideration, so the value here is ₦800,000 (NTA Section 149(1)(a)).
The VAT in the ₦860,000 payment is ₦60,000 (NTA Sections 148 and 149(1)(a)).
must_not: gives the VAT as ₦64,500 by applying 7.5% to the VAT-inclusive amount

question: Our company makes and sells furniture, does not provide professional services and is not part of a multinational group. For a year of assessment under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, its gross turnover was ₦320,000,000, its total fixed assets were ₦180,000,000 and its total profits were ₦45,000,000. How much company income tax is due on those profits?
expected_answer: A small company has gross turnover of ₦50,000,000 or less and total fixed assets not exceeding ₦250,000,000; with turnover of ₦320,000,000 this company is not a small company (NTA Section 202, "small company").
A company that is not small pays tax at 30% of its total profits (NTA Section 56(b)).
The tax due is 30% of ₦45,000,000, which is ₦13,500,000 (NTA Section 56(b)).
must_not: applies the 0% small company rate
adds the development levy into the company income tax figure
rationale: Hand working: turnover 320,000,000 > 50,000,000, so not small (the assets test does not save it); tax = 45,000,000 x 0.30 = 13,500,000.00. Section 57 does not arise: the company is not part of a multinational group (Section 57(2)(a)) and its turnover is far below ₦20 billion (Section 57(2)(b)). The year is one under the 2025 Act, so the 30% rate in Section 56(b) applies.

question: Our Nigerian company is not a small company, is not a non-resident company and has no petroleum operations. Its assessable profits for the year are ₦72,500,000. How much development levy does it pay?
expected_answer: A development levy of 4% is imposed on the assessable profits of companies other than small companies and non-resident companies (NTA Section 59(1)).
The levy is 4% of ₦72,500,000, which is ₦2,900,000 (NTA Section 59(1)).
must_not: states that the company is exempt from the levy
applies a rate other than 4%

question: Our company paid ₦3,400,000 of company income tax after the due date. Leaving interest aside, what sum is added to the tax for paying late?
expected_answer: Where tax is not paid within the prescribed period, a sum equal to 10% of the tax payable is added to it (NTAA Section 65(1)(a)).
The sum added is 10% of ₦3,400,000, which is ₦340,000 (NTAA Section 65(1)(a)).
must_not: states a numeric figure for the interest
applies a rate other than 10%
rationale: Hand working: 3,400,000 x 0.10 = 340,000.00. The question sets interest aside, so the interest rule is not a key point. Optional proviso: interest also runs on naira tax at the Central Bank of Nigeria monetary policy rate plus a spread set by the Minister (NTAA Section 65(1)(b)); an answer may mention it but is not marked down for leaving it out.

question: Our company did not file a required tax return, and the failure went on for five months in total before we filed. What administrative penalty applies for the whole period?
expected_answer: A taxable person that fails to file returns is liable to ₦100,000 for the first month of the failure and ₦50,000 for each later month it continues (NTAA Section 101).
For five months the penalty is ₦100,000 plus 4 x ₦50,000, which is ₦300,000 (NTAA Section 101).
must_not: uses the failure-to-register amounts of ₦50,000 and ₦25,000
charges ₦100,000 for every month
rationale: Hand working: first month 100,000 + four later months x 50,000 = 100,000 + 200,000 = 300,000.00.

question: Our company made a taxable sale on which the VAT due was ₦90,000, but it did not record that sale on the fiscalisation system. Leaving interest aside, what administrative penalty applies?
expected_answer: A taxable person that fails to process a taxable supply through the fiscalisation system is liable to ₦200,000 plus 100% of the tax due, and interest at the Central Bank of Nigeria monetary policy rate (NTAA Section 104).
Leaving interest aside, the penalty is ₦200,000 plus ₦90,000, which is ₦290,000 (NTAA Section 104).
must_not: states a numeric figure for the interest
gives the penalty as ₦200,000 only
